title: Yoga (revisited)
hook: a brown line worn across a green lawn, and Vyasa's wheel of thoughts and traces

segments.voice: Yesterday Yoga showed where it parts from Samkhya: Ishvara, the purusha never caught, teacher of even the earliest teachers. Whose teaching did you use without thinking? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

Outside a library, a brown line runs across the lawn. Nobody planned it. There's a paved walkway that goes around the corner, but someone once cut across the grass to save a few steps. Then someone else followed, because the grass was a little flatter there. Then everyone after. Now the line is bare dirt, and new feet take it without deciding to. The path made the walking, and the walking made the path. Vyasa's commentary on Yoga describes the mind working exactly like that lawn, and gives the loop a name.
screen: `A LINE ACROSS THE LAWN.` → `NOBODY PLANNED IT.` → `THE WALKING MAKES THE PATH.`

segments.voice: The name is samskara. In the Yoga Sutras it means the trace an experience leaves behind in the mind, like a footprint in grass. Patanjali's word for the mind's movements is vritti, a turning. Vyasa, commenting on the early sutras, ties the two together in a loop. Turnings leave traces, he says, and traces give rise to turnings again. And so the wheel of turnings and traces keeps going round, without pause. That's the lawn. A worry shows up, it leaves a groove, and the groove makes the next worry easier to have. It's not a moral failing. It's how minds work, in Yoga's account. So what can be done about a path worn that deep? You can't argue a lawn out of its line. Here's the hopeful turn, near the end of the first chapter. Patanjali says that a trace born of true insight blocks the other traces. He means a deep insight, not one good afternoon. But the principle carries: the mechanism that wore the old path can wear a new one. Read in a small way, every time attention comes back to the breath, every time a sharp reply gets a second look, that's a footstep somewhere new. That's why Yoga cares so much about doing things again and again. Not because repetition is a virtue in itself, but because that's how a lawn changes. And notice the word. Samskara has other homes in Hindu life too. The same word names the rites that mark a life, from naming a child to a wedding. In Yoga, it means something quieter: the grooves underneath the next thought.
screen: `TURNINGS LEAVE TRACES.` · `TRACES MAKE TURNINGS.` · `A NEW TRACE BLOCKS THE OLD.` · `EVERY RETURN IS A FOOTSTEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk a new path for two minutes. Sit, and let your breath settle. Choose one place to rest attention, the breath in the belly. The mind will wander down its old lines, the usual worry, the usual plan. That's fine. Each time you notice, come back to the belly. Don't count the wanderings. Count, if anything, the returns. Each one is a step across new grass. If you pray, you can let each return be a small offering. The bell holds the time.
Yoga. Vyasa's wheel: turnings leave traces and traces make turnings, and a trace of insight can block the old ones. Samskara is the trace.

Your line: Yoga, revisited. Today, catch one thought that arrives on its own well-worn path, and take one step somewhere new, a different response, however small. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn Vyasa's picture of the wheel of turnings and traces, and teachers use it to explain why steady, repeated practice matters: each return of attention lays down a new trace.

match.prompt: the wheel in Yoga — tap the pairs.
pairs: turnings make traces, traces make turnings

turnings leave traces, and traces give rise to turnings again.
Patanjali says old traces can never be changed
he says a trace born of true insight blocks the other traces.

fork.setup: the same worry keeps arriving, on the same worn path. in Yoga's account, what changes the lawn?
options: arguing the worry away once and for all
laying down new traces, one return at a time
fork.reveal: new traces. Patanjali says a trace born of insight blocks the others, which is why Yoga cares so much about coming back again and again.

original.note: Sanskrit: in Yoga, the trace an experience leaves in the mind; elsewhere in Hindu life, a rite that marks a life.

trapdoor: what you thought: samskara is a ceremony, like a naming or a wedding.
what it means: in Yoga it's also the trace an experience leaves in the mind, the groove the next thought runs along.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa's wheel of vritti and samskara, each producing the other, and Yoga Sutra 1.50, where a trace born of insight blocks the rest.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.5 (turnings produce traces and traces produce turnings; the wheel turns ceaselessly)
Yoga Sutras 1.50 (the trace born of truth-bearing insight obstructs other traces)

notes: Confirm the vritti-samskara-chakra passage is in Vyasa's comment on 1.5 (the script says 'commenting on the early sutras' to stay safe).
Samskara also names the life-cycle rites (namakarana, vivaha and others); stated briefly without listing a count. Check the wording.
'The only way a lawn ever changes' is the script's own image, not a claim about the text; editors may soften.

Editor: superlative 'Yoga's oldest commentary' cut from the hook; 'only way' cut; 1.50 no longer implies every small return is the insight-born trace (now 'read in a small way'); 'day and night' changed to 'without pause' to match the Bhashya's sense.
